claims.claim: In 1956 Warwick Kerr arranged for 63 African queens to be brought to Brazil, of which 48 survived at the quarantine apiary near Rio Claro.
claims.episode_span: In 1956 he arranged for 63 queens to be brought from southern Africa, of which 48 survived the journey to an experimental apiary near Rio Claro, São Paulo
claims.source_title: Africanized Honey Bee - Utah County Beekeepers Association
claims.supporting_quote: Kerr was able to acquire 63 live queens from South African beekeepers. These were later taken to a quarantine area at an agricultural research station near Rio Claro, where 48 queens survived till the next year.

claims.claim: In 1957, 26 swarms with their queens escaped from the experimental apiary in Brazil.
claims.episode_span: In October 1957, a beekeeper in Rio Claro, São Paulo state, noticed that twenty-six colonies had vanished from their screened hives
claims.supporting_quote: African honey bees were first introduced to Brazil in 1956 to increase honey production, but 26 swarms with their queens escaped from their experimental apiary in 1957.

claims.claim: The October 1957 escape happened because the queen excluders fitted to the hives were removed, releasing 26 swarms.
claims.episode_span: The escape itself was ordinary—queen excluders removed from the hives during routine work—but the biological properties the bees carried
claims.supporting_quote: in October 1957 a visiting beekeeper, noticing that the queen excluders were interfering with the worker bees' movement, removed them, resulting in the accidental release of 26 Tanganyikan swarms

claims.claim: Kerr's goal was to breed a bee strain that would produce more honey in tropical conditions than the European strains then in use in the Americas.
claims.episode_span: Warwick E. Kerr, a Brazilian geneticist trained in the United States, wanted to improve honey production in the tropics
claims.supporting_quote: Kerr was attempting to breed a strain of bees that would produce more honey in tropical conditions than the European strain of honey bee then in use

claims.claim: The first wild colony of Africanized honey bees in the United States was found near Hidalgo, Texas, in 1990.
claims.episode_span: the first colonies reached the United States near Hidalgo, Texas, in 1990
claims.source_title: Africanized Honey Bee - Utah County Beekeepers Association
claims.supporting_quote: the first wild colony of Africanized honey bees was found in the United States, near Hidalgo, Texas
